papers.title: Reproducible variability: assessing human vs. AI discordance in attempting to reproduce the same observational study
papers.abstract: Objective: Previously, nine expert teams given a published study and identical code sets produced nine substantially different cohorts, prompting the conclusion that analytic code cannot be reliably generated from natural-language description. We tested whether an artificial intelligence (AI) agent, given that same description, reproduces a cohort definition more faithfully and consistently than those teams. Materials and Methods: Against a claims database of 35.9 million patients, we executed 27 independent reproductions of that published glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist cohort definition: the nine published human definitions re-implemented deterministically (Arm A); nine independent AI agent runs given the source paper as published (Arm B); and nine given a rewrite that removed its internal contradictions (Arm C). All arms received identical frozen code sets. Agreement with a reference cohort was quantified by the Jaccard index. Results: Agents in Arm B achieved a median Jaccard index of 0.450 versus 0.259 for the human definitions, median pairwise agreement of 0.492 versus 0.149, and a 5.06-fold versus 32.0-fold size spread. Agent variation resolved almost entirely onto two criteria reported differently in the source main text and supplement. In Arm C, median agreement and median pairwise agreement both reached 1.000. Discussion: Changing only the analyst strongly trended towards improvement in fidelity, with every agent run more self-consistent than every human team. Changing the specification resulted in exact fidelity and self-consistency. Irreproducibility arose from both specification quality and inter-analyst variation. Conclusion: AI agents were more consistent than human teams when translating published natural-language descriptions into code.

papers.title: MedDx, a training-free AI phenotyping model, identifies alcohol use disorder in cirrhosis with hepatologist-level agreement
papers.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is often under-documented in patients with cirrhosis, which delays treatment. Expert chart review of clinical notes can identify under-documented AUD, but is not scalable. We propose MedDx, an open-weight, training-free, and engine-agnostic language model, to phenotype AUD using clinical notes in patients with cirrhosis. We benchmarked MedDx on a 485-patient study cohort sampled from the 14,406-patient Indiana Cirrhosis Registry, using a chart-review-based reference as ground truth. MedDx agreed with the ground truth at three-class Cohen's {kappa} 0.92, against 0.67 for the AUD diagnosis code. It agreed with one hepatologist at 0.85 on all 485 charts and with a second at 0.82 on 186 charts, on which the two hepatologists agreed at 0.87. Weighted to the registry, its sensitivity was 98% and specificity 94%, against 63% and 96% for the AUD diagnosis code, and 61% of an estimated 6,223 patients with AUD had no AUD diagnosis by the first cirrhosis diagnosis. MedDx is openly available as an off-the-shelf, equitable, and auditable tool to identify AUD.

papers.title: How many large language models does title-abstract screening need? Theory, two replications and an evaluation at real prevalence
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Researchers increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) to screen titles and abstracts, assuming that more models make screening safer. We estimated how many models a screening ensemble needs, given correlated errors, and tested the answer on independent reviews and at real prevalence. Methods: We modelled correlated votes with a beta-binomial model and estimated, by bootstrap, the smallest ensemble capturing 95% of the net-benefit gain attainable over the best single model, accounting for human reading time and machine cost. Eleven LLMs from four developers voted blind on records from 13 SYNERGY reviews (derivation). We tested predictions fixed in advance on 10 and 16 Cochrane reviews from a public screening benchmark (replications) and evaluated a two-voter pipeline with an adjudicator on 11 complete benchmark collections and six reviews published in 2026. Results: Errors on relevant records were correlated (intraclass correlation 0.56 among eight different models; 0.75-0.78 among roles or copies of one model): eight models carried the information of about 1.6 independent ones. In derivation, the best single model, pair and trio reached sensitivities of 0.920, 0.975 and 0.981. Three or fewer models captured 95% of the attainable gain in at least 86%, 88% and 80.8% of bootstrap replicates of every scenario in the derivation set and the two replications, respectively. Six of seven registered predictions held in replication 1 and three of five sealed predictions in replication 2, where a fourth model added 2.1 percentage points to trios on average but 0.3 to the best trio. At real prevalence, the pipeline sent 94 of 96 included studies to human reading in the benchmark collections and 163 of 178 in the 2026 reviews (12.1% of 12,196 records sent to reading); its more sensitive voter alone sent 259 of 274 with 12.0%, at under a quarter of the machine cost. Conclusion: Because LLM errors are correlated, our results suggest two or three well-chosen models may suffice, but this needs deeper exploration in future studies. Which models are combined and how matter as much as how many, and any ensemble should be compared with its best single member.

papers.title: DiabetIA: A Longitudinal Electronic Health Record Dataset for Diabetes Research from Mexico
papers.abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) from primary care are scarce in low- and middle-income countries, and few have been made available to researchers in Latin America. We present DiabetIA, a longitudinal dataset derived from the primary care records of the Mexican Institute of Social Security (IMSS). The first release comprises 136,674 adults followed in six IMSS family medicine units in the state of Michoacan between 2005 and 2020, with more than 3.2 million visits summarized in 414,770 two-year windows with at least one visit. Each window includes demographics, ICD-10 diagnoses, anthropometry, vital signs, laboratory results and prescriptions, and type 2 diabetes diagnoses in the following year as prediction targets. At baseline, 24.4% of the patients had type 2 diabetes, 37.1% hypertension and 32.3% obesity. Technical validation assessed completeness, plausibility, consistency, temporal coverage and agreement with a state health survey. DiabetIA is freely available for download to support research on chronic disease trajectories and prediction in an underrepresented population.

papers.title: LifeLine.ai: A SigLIP-MedGemma Multimodal Framework with KTO Alignment for Open-Vocabulary 12-Lead ECG Report Generation
papers.abstract: Automated twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has historically relied on discriminative classifiers limited to closed-set diagnostic labels, signal reconstruction, or saliency heatmaps. While categorizing predefined arrhythmias well, these static classifiers cannot generate narrative clinical reports, incorporate patient history, or support interactive clinical question-answering (Q&A). We present LifeLine.ai, an end-toend multimodal Vision-ECG-Language framework for automated cardiac diagnosis and clinical reporting. After early attempts at waveform peak-tracking and coordinate mapping failed against complex morphological variations, we leveraged large-scale PhysioNet repositories (MIMIC-IV and PTB-XL). Because hardware limits precluded training on over 800,000 raw records, we curated a balanced subset to estimate performance, converting one-dimensional signals into 3x4 twelve-lead grids with continuous Lead II rhythm strips at the bottom. Our pipeline integrates YOLOv11s localization, a LoRAadapted Google SigLIP encoder, a trainable Multi-Layer Perceptron projector, and a 4-bit quantized MedGemma-4B model, complemented by a separate Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) pipeline built on collected user feedback and a multi-LLM consensus engine. On this compact subset, SigLIP outperformed Swin Transformer encodings (~0.21 vs. ~0.25 validation loss), achieving 71.0% open-vocabulary precision and a 75.0% contextual F1 score across a cloud deployment spanning Vercel, mobile apps, Amazon EC2, Firebase, Hugging Face, Modal GPUs, and lifelinecg-sdk. Our code is available at https://github.com/Asad939asad/ LifeLine.ai-.

papers.title: An Explainable Analytics Framework for Identifying Process Deviations in Emergency Care for Patients with Multiple Long-Term Conditions
papers.abstract: Patients with Multiple Long-Term Conditions (MLTCs), also known as multimorbidity, often present clinical and operational challenges in emergency departments (EDs), yet how their care pathways deviate from expected workflows remains underexplored. This study introduces a process-aware analytical framework that quantifies and interprets ED process deviations by integrating multi-perspective conformance checking with explainable machine learning. Using routinely collected Scottish ED data between 2017-2023, we derived an empirical benchmark pathway. We introduced a new metric, the deviation score (DS), which captures both structural misalignments and breaches of the four-hour ED standard, a national service target defined as completion of ED care within four hours of arrival. Compared with non-MLTC attendances, MLTC patients exhibited longer and more complex pathways, higher DS values, and lower conformance to the benchmark model. The framework enabled interpretable SHAP analyses, revealing that deviation severity among MLTC attendances was primarily associated with triage acuity, year of attendance, activity queue length (number of patients queuing for the same care activity), and referral source, with additional contributions from age, arrival time, and number of chronic conditions. Threshold effects were observed in both queue length and multimorbidity burden, beyond which deviation severity increased sharply, suggesting points where standard pathways become harder to maintain. These findings show that deviation severity for MLTC patients is shaped by clinical urgency and system-level pressures at presentation. However, the inherent complexity of MLTC patients may further increase vulnerability to deviation. The framework offers the potential foundation for process evaluation and targeted improvement in emergency care.

papers.title: Making Invisible Infrastructure Visible: Data Landscapes Across a National Pain and Opioid Research Network through a Qualitative Assessment
papers.abstract: Background Multi-site research networks have become central infrastructure for NIH-supported health research, yet network-level coordination has focused on harmonization, common data models and FAIR principles, while rarely characterizing the heterogeneous data landscapes within a network first. The Helping to End Addiction Long-term(R) Initiative (HEAL Initiative) Data2Action (HD2A) program comprises ten autonomously designed innovation and acceleration projects in opioid use disorder treatment and pain management, with no pre-existing network-level view of what data each project used or how it was governed. Objectives To make the HD2A data-infrastructure landscape visible by systematically characterizing the data environments of all ten projects and identifying cross-project themes, coordination opportunities, and lessons for multi-site networks. Methods Data Infrastructure Support Center staff extracted each project's data-environment characteristics from project documentation into a structured 15-element assessment, which project investigators reviewed and corrected. Two analysts independently coded the ten validated assessments (two-pass inductive content analysis; 19-code codebook), developed six cross-project themes from the coded passages by consensus, and judged each project against them. An investigator reflection survey, summarized descriptively, contextualized the document-based findings. Results Six themes characterized the landscape: all projects integrate multi-source, cross-sector data; dashboards are the common data-to-action venue; adoption of standards-based interoperability is uneven; governance complexity increases nonlinearly with institutional partners; implementation and improvement science frameworks serve as data-quality scaffolding; and sustainability plans depend on institutional transfer. Five synergy clusters were identified. Investigators consistently described data access and governance, not analytic capability, as the binding constraint, and distinguished sustaining technical products from sustaining their use. Conclusions Making a networks data infrastructure visible is not a substitute for harmonization but a prerequisite for deciding how and what to harmonize. HD2As autonomously designed projects share a common structure of constraints, creating opportunities for coordination without uniformity. The structured elicitation approach is replicable in other innovation networks.

papers.title: Tabular Foundation AI Models in Healthcare: A WHO-Inspired Benchmark for Responsible AI and Trustworthiness
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly used for structured prediction, yet their suitability for healthcare applications remains uncertain because predictive performance alone does not establish fairness, probabilistic reliability, or robustness. We developed a multidimensional benchmark to compare four TFMs: TabFM, TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICL, against Logistic Regression and XGBoost across a curated, standardized suite of ten WHO-aligned healthcare classification datasets across diverse disease domains. Additionally, we harmonized clinical schemas, standardized protected sex attributes and outcome targets, and released both balanced-scale and natural-prevalence variants of the datasets to establish a benchmarking resource in healthcare machine learning. All models were evaluated using identical five-fold stratified cross-validation partitions and standardized preprocessing. Performance was assessed using 20 metrics spanning predictive discrimination, sex-based fairness, probability calibration, and robustness to Gaussian feature perturbations. A composite Clinical Model Evaluation Score (CMES) was used to summarize performance across these dimensions. Google TabFM achieved the highest mean CMES (0.8811), followed closely by TabDPT (0.8796), TabICL (0.8775), TabPFN (0.8756), XGBoost (0.8650), and Logistic Regression (0.8549). The Friedman test indicated significant differences among models ({chi}2F (5) = 24.914, p = 1.45 x 10^-4; Kendalls W = 0.498). However, post-hoc comparisons revealed no statistically significant differences among the four TFMs after Holm correction. TFMs generally demonstrated stronger discrimination and probabilistic calibration than conventional baselines, with TabFM achieving the highest mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (0.9327) and the lowest expected calibration error (0.0674). Conversely, Logistic Regression exhibited the greatest stability under feature perturbations, while fairness performance varied substantially across datasets and models. These findings highlight the potential of TFMs for small-data healthcare prediction while demonstrating that their advantages are dimension-dependent. Multidimensional, dataset-specific evaluation and external validation remain essential before clinical implementation. All analysis codes, original datasets, and multiple variants of benchmark datasets are publicly available in a GitHub repository to ensure reproducibility and future research.

papers.title: Leveraging HCUP Data to Predict Preventable Admissions in Patients with Chronic Kidney Diseases
papers.abstract: ObjectivesThis study developed machine learning (ML) to predict 90-day preventable admissions in CKD patients while evaluating racial disparities in model performance. Materials and MethodsStudy population included CKD patients ([≥]18 years) with hospital encounters in Maryland (2016-2023). Logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), XGBoost, and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) models were used to predict 90-day preventable admissions after a CKD outpatient visit. Data used in this study was extracted from Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP). Results28,214 unique patients were included, of whom 3974 (14%) experienced a subsequent preventable admission. LR achieved comparable performance with RF and XGBoost (AuROC 0.784 - 0.788, AuPRC 0.397 - 0.416), outperforming KNN (AuROC 0.753, AuPRC 0.342). All models performed marginally better in the Black population (AuROC 0.773 - 0.807, AuPRC 0.369 - 0.467) than in the white population (AuROC 0.738 - 0.776, AuPRC 0.329 - 0.394). The false negative rates (FNR) in the white population were higher across different models (Black: 0.236 - 0.33, white: 0.297 - 0.377). DiscussionOur results suggest that LR can achieve comparable prediction performances than tree-based ML algorithms. Hospital utilization and congestive heart failure are among the most important predictors across models. Further analyses on prediction bias revealed that FNRs are more significant in white patients, which can be due to their overall lower utilization. ConclusionsThis study demonstrated a pipeline to develop ML models predicting preventable admissions while revealing existing racial biases. These findings can inform ambulatory settings on how to reduce preventable admissions among CKD patients.

papers.title: Evaluating Prominent Machine Translation Models for Kinyarwanda to English for Patient-Provider Conversations
papers.abstract: BackgroundLinguistic barriers between patients and providers cause diagnostic error, poor adherence, and adverse events, and disproportionately affect speakers of low-resource languages. Kinyarwanda, spoken by more than 20 million people, has a small digital footprint, and the quality of off-the-shelf machine translation (MT) for its clinical dialogue is poorly documented. MethodsWe evaluated six MT systems (GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Azure Translate, Google Translate, and NLLB-200) for Kinyarwanda-to-English patient-provider conversations. Using a professional reference corpus of 600 conversations, stratified across three pandemic periods and collected in Rwanda via the WelTel platform, we assessed automated metrics (semantic similarity, BLEU, chrF, and translation edit rate [TER]) and 0-100 quality ratings from three professional Kinyarwanda-English translators, with reliability quantified by intraclass correlation (ICC). De-identified secondary data were approved by UBC (H20-01031) and the Rwanda National Ethics Committee (100/RNEC/2020). FindingsOn the full 600-conversation cohort, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash had closely clustered semantic similarity (0.877, 0.874, 0.873), well above Azure Translate (0.809) and NLLB-200 (0.754); Gemini 2.5 Flash led on BLEU (43.13) and the lowest TER (68.15). Translators ranked GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash highest (means 81.55 and 81.51), then GPT-4o-mini (72.67), Azure Translate (55.16), and NLLB-200 (39.05); average-rater reliability was moderate (ICC 0.594, rising to 0.701 on a balanced 85-conversation subset). Automated n-gram metrics understated the quality gap human raters perceived between large language models and conventional systems. InterpretationGPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash are the strongest off-the-shelf systems for Kinyarwanda-English clinical translation and primary choices for human-in-the-loop use, with GPT-4o-mini a cost-efficient alternative. NLLB-200 underperformed, showing that models built for low-resource languages are not automatically suited to specialised clinical domains without fine-tuning. Human evaluation should be prioritised over automated metrics alone when comparing LLM-based translation.

papers.title: Community pharmacy responses to online reviews: a national cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Objectives: Online reviews constitute a source of information on the experience of users in community pharmacies. The way in which pharmacists engage with them remains poorly documented. The objective was to describe the frequency, determinants, and content of the responses provided by French pharmacy teams to reviews published on Google Maps. Methods: Cross-sectional observational study. Public reviews from nearly all French community pharmacies (approximately 20 000) were collected automatically between September and October 2026. For each review, the rating, the text of the review, the time since its publication, and the text of the response, if it existed, were collected. Factors associated with the response were studied using logistic regression. Sentiment of the reviews and the tone of the responses were automatically coded according to a predefined grid. The presence of reviews generated by artificial intelligence, as well as potential interventions on the ratings, were explored.newline Results: In total, 1 008 024 extractions (729 521 reviews and 278 504 responses) concerning 19 985 pharmacies were analysed. A response was present for 38% of reviews and 67.5% of pharmacies had responded at least once. The response rate was higher for negative reviews (one or two stars) than for positive reviews (five stars) (adjusted OR 1.35; 95% CI [1.33--1.38]; adjusted risk difference +3.6 percentage points; 95% CI [3.3--3.8]), and these responses were approximately twice as long (adjusted geometric mean ratio 3.03; 95% CI [3.01--3.06]). The tone of the responses was very widely judged to be appropriate. Comments generated by artificial intelligence seem to be appearing progressively and represent approximately 3-4% in 2026. The removal of poor ratings appears to be marginal. Conclusions: Community pharmacists regularly and appropriately respond to online reviews, including, and in particular, less positive ones. These results could serve in the development of specific professional recommendations aimed at securing this practice.

papers.title: Optimizing Sepsis Treatment via Latent Protocol Inference
papers.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency characterized by high mortality and variable treatment practices. Optimizing treatment from retrospective data is challenging due to sparse, delayed outcomes and complex physiological dynamics. We introduce the Generative Latent Protocol Model (GLPM), a probabilistic framework that structures clinical decision-making through a latent protocol variable anchored on the patients admission state. This latent variable acts as an information bottleneck, decoupling the generation of treatment trajectories from the prediction of survival outcomes. Unlike methods that rely on value estimation or noisy return-to-go conditioning, our model is trained via Maximum Likelihood Estimation to capture the joint distribution of treatment trajectories and outcomes. At inference time, we treat treatment optimization as a probabilistic inverse problem: we sample latent protocols from a posterior distribution conditioned on a target survival probability. On the ICU-Sepsis benchmark derived from MIMIC-III, our best variant matches or exceeds eight offline baselines on all five datasets, with gains that are statistically significant against every baseline on the most heterogeneous dataset, and it offers interpretability through patient-specific counterfactual analysis.

papers.title: Concerns over spillover, exclusions, and hospital unit differences in an AI early warning system trial (CONCERN-EWS)
papers.abstract: Rossetti et al. report that hospitalized patients whose care was informed by an AI-based clinical deterioration early warning system (EWS) were 36% less likely to die during a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial when compared to patients on usual care units without the EWS (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.53-0.78).1 The authors should be applauded for conducting a trial evaluating the effect of an AI intervention on patient health outcomes; more such trials are needed. Several aspects of the study, however, raise concerns that its findings may not accurately reflect the effect of the EWS. First, spillover effects on availability of scarce intensive care unit (ICU) beds could have led to worse outcomes for patients in the control group. Second, EWS-informed clinical decisions may have led to more frequent exclusion of high-risk patients from the intervention group. Either of these concerns could have led to overestimation of AI benefit. Finally, large pre-trial differences in hospital unit mortality rates suggest that unreported cluster-level imbalance or between-cluster variance could also have affected trial results.

papers.title: Effect of a feedback loop on clinical prediction model performance
papers.abstract: Clinical prediction models (CPMs) that guide treatment-initiation, and therefore affect patient outcomes, may create feedback loops when updated using data from patients whose care they influenced. Treatment can alter predictor-outcome relationships and outcome prevalence, potentially reducing model performance. This simulation study aims to quantify this effect using setting parameters based on cardiovascular disease prediction and intervention and assess if including a treatment variable in the model mitigates any performance degradation. In the simulation, models were developed to predict the probability of a binary adverse outcome, guide treatment allocation, and then updated using data containing patients in whom the model was applied. Scenarios varied treatment inclusion as a predictor in the model and the presence of unmeasured confounding. Performance was assessed with calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, c-statistic, and correct risk assignment relative to treatment threshold. Without unmeasured confounding, excluding treatment as a predictor resulted in miscalibration, but including treatment solves this problem completely. With unmeasured confounding, performance deteriorated even when treatment was included. These results agree with previous findings and illustrate the likelihood that models that guide interventions may experience performance deterioration due to the difficulty of recording treatment and avoiding unmeasured confounders. Causal inference methods combined with risk prediction may help address this problem. Further research is needed on monitoring techniques to allow detection of this issue post-model implementation.

papers.title: STREAM: Sequential Transformer for Risk Estimation from Asynchronous Medical Events for Dynamic Postoperative AKI Prediction
papers.abstract: Postoperative acute kidney injury (PO-AKI) risk estimates evolve as clinical information accumulates, yet many electronic health record (EHR) models use static or fixed-window representations. We developed STREAM, a perioperative event-stream Transformer that represents irregular EHR data as chronological clinical events and supports surgery-index prediction at surgery completion and event-by-event postoperative AKI prediction. In a retrospective cohort of 167,078 noncardiac surgical episodes, STREAM achieved surgery-index AUROC/AUPRC of 0.942/0.771, the Time-series Transformer 0.933/0.729, and GRU-D 0.926/0.695. Postoperative macro-AUPRC across 6-hour evaluation intervals was 0.589, 0.525, and 0.547, respectively. STREAM showed more consistent calibration across postoperative time points than the comparators. Event-arrival attribution and within-window permutation analysis enabled event-level interpretation of how newly arrived information and fine-grained event ordering shaped evolving risk estimates. These findings support event-stream modeling as an interpretable framework for dynamic, temporally resolved prediction from longitudinal EHR data as well as a potential risk-estimation component for future perioperative digital twins.

papers.title: Continually pretrained open-weight language models can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based clinical prediction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) prompted with electronic health record (EHR) data have predicted clinical outcomes less accurately than locally trained machine-learning models. We developed VEX-EHR by extending the vocabulary of a 12-billion-parameter open-weight LLM (weights publicly available) with 17,601 clinical and audit-log codes from 170,483 patients records at one academic medical center, continuing its pretraining on those 2019-2024 records (4.7 billion tokens) and fine-tuning it per task. AUROCs were 0.917 for next-24-hour discharge, 0.715 for 30-day readmission and 0.847 for intensive care unit acute kidney injury, against 0.868, 0.677 and 0.828 for gradient-boosted trees and 0.848, 0.650 and 0.791 for CEHR-BERT, an EHR foundation model. Continued pretraining added 0.031-0.053 AUROC on every task. With 10% of the labels, VEX-EHR exceeded both comparators using all labels for discharge, and CEHR-BERT for readmission, valuable where labels are costly. Adapted by continued pretraining, open-weight LLMs can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based prediction.

papers.title: Co-occurrence Is Not Evidence: Separating Protein-Disease Findings from Incidental Mentions in HFpEF Literature
papers.abstract: Literature-mining pipelines such as CaseOLAP rank proteins by how often they appear next to a disease term. Appearing next to a disease is not the same as being implicated in it: in our 300-sentence held-out set of PubMed sentences that mention a protein and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), only 115 assert a biological association. The rest report a negative finding or mention the protein in passing, for example as a drug the patients were taking. We train a sentence-level filter that sorts each protein mention into associated, not_associated or incidental. It is a fine-tuned PubMedBERT trained with class-weighted cross-entropy and R-Drop regularization, combined into a six-model majority-vote ensemble over three random seeds. On the held-out set, with no thresholds tuned on it, the ensemble reaches 85.3% accuracy and 86.1% macro F1 (bootstrap 95% confidence intervals 81.0-89.3% and 82.1-89.7%), against 38.3% accuracy for the co-occurrence baseline, which counts every mention as an association. Single models average 84.4 {+/-} 0.7% accuracy across seeds. Run after CaseOLAP, the filter removes protein mentions that are not evidence of association from the HFpEF candidate list. Where the ensembles majority vote disagreed with the annotation, the annotation was often wrong. Expert review of those sentences corrected 53 of 88 flagged evaluation labels and 109 training labels. Most of the errors came from one flaw in the annotation sheet: in sentences naming several proteins, it did not say which protein the label was for. The audit stage coincided with the largest accuracy gain in the project, but the same stage also changed the evaluation labels and the training loss, so we report it as a chronology, not as a controlled result.

papers.title: rendehR: a cohort-first, provenance-aware, agentic-ready pipeline for harmonizing multi-source electronic health records
papers.abstract: ObjectivePublic electronic health record (EHR) databases differ in schema, identifiers, coding systems, units, and event structure, making disease-specific studies across multiple sources difficult to construct and audit. We developed rendehR, a computational pipeline and R package for cohort-centered extraction and harmonization of multi-source EHR data. Materials and MethodsrendehR treats cohort definition as an explicit executable component of dataset construction. Cohorts can be defined using diagnosis codes, identifiers, R callbacks, or source-specific SQL. After cohort selection, linked source tables are restricted to the selected population and can be retained as cohort-specific Parquet datasets or loaded into a persistent database. Clinical concepts are defined using source-aware mappings, generated, or curated SQL and are harmonized into flat, time-series, and duration representations. Configuration, executable SQL, cohort metadata, concept-origin metadata, and source-level values are retained to support inspection and traceability. In the current version rendehR provides interactive R assistant wizards for workflow configuration, a Shiny application for patient-level data visualization, three agent skills for AI-assisted workflow execution and extension, and an MCP server exposing nine read- only tools for AI-assisted configuration, concept discovery, and cohort exploration. The current implementation supports MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU-CRD. We demonstrate rendehR on a reference cohort of spinal cord injury and disease (SCID). ResultsUsing the reference cohort, rendehR identified 4,320, 39,850, and 2,343 qualifying hospital admissions in MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU-CRD, respectively. Patient-level extraction expanded these cohorts to 5,725, 104,988, and 2,823 hospital admissions, with 5,983, 17,405, and 3,441 associated ICU stays, respectively. Applying the more complex Sepsis-3 case identification, rendehR identified and extracted 34,460, 41,296, and 47,035 qualifying ICU stays across the same databases, respectively. The current concept library includes 22 flat, 123 time- series, and 75 duration harmonized concepts. ConclusionrendehR provides a cohort-centered framework for constructing disease-specific datasets from multiple heterogeneous EHR sources while preserving the source-specific logic used to define cohorts and clinical concepts. The package supports reusable cohort artifacts, inspectable SQL-based concept construction, harmonized analytical representations, and traceable study- specific data pipelines. papers.title: The unedited acceptance rate: a review-fidelity metric for human-in-the-loop clinical AI
papers.abstract: ObjectiveGuidance for large language model (LLM) drafting in clinical care relies on human review, yet review is rarely measured as a control. We aimed to define computable measures of review fidelity, establish which a deployed system can compute, and pre-specify their first analysis. Materials and MethodsFor a multi-agent clinical system in routine use at one private London outpatient clinic, we defined acceptance coverage, attribution completeness, the unedited acceptance rate (UAR), a bounded normalized edit distance, availability latency and an unedited fast-approval rate (UFA). We checked each measure against the systems code and database structure at a fixed commit on four approval routes and pre-specified a prospective 12-week analysis. ResultsThe UAR equals the mass at zero of the edit-distance distribution, and availability latency bounds reading time from above only. Clinical documentation keeps draft and signed text with a recorded signer, so the core measures are computable there. Help-desk edit telemetry is written only when the agents version has been stored. The WhatsApp agent route records no edit signal, and its approver need not be named. No route records when a draft is opened. Documentation accept events were not written before a change committed on November 16, 2026. Model-generated content, including live voice-agent speech, also reaches patients without approval. No measured values are reported. DiscussionAcceptance alone cannot separate accurate drafts from approval without reading, and three of four routes cannot yet support the family. ConclusionReview fidelity can be specified as telemetry at the approval event. Validation against missed errors is required.

papers.title: Task-specific fine-tuning versus frontier large language models for RoB 2 risk of bias assessment: development and external benchmark evaluation of RoB-BERT
papers.abstract: BackgroundResearchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to assess risk of bias in randomized trials, but how task-specific fine-tuned models compare with frontier models remains uncertain. ObjectiveTo develop RoB-BERT, a fine-tuned RoB 2 assessment system, and to compare its agreement with human assessments against that of three frontier LLMs. MethodsRoB 2 rates five bias domains and the trial overall as low risk, some concerns or high risk, based on answers to 22 signalling questions. RoB-BERT answers each question, quotes the supporting sentences from the trial report, and applies the official RoB 2 algorithm. We trained RoB-BERT on 5,304 reviewer-checked assessments, none from a test trial, and compared it with Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon, each given identical prompts and text, against 419 published human assessments (ROBoto2, LogiMed-RoB and Cochrane reviews) made without AI assistance. Each reference was the single published judgement for that trial, made by one assessor or agreed by two, rather than an expert reference standard, so we also report agreement between two human assessors of the same trial. ResultsIn ROBoto2, pairs of human assessors who rated the same trial agreed on 61.2% to 64.7% of domain judgements ({kappa} 0.15 to 0.35) and 46.2% to 50.0% of overall judgements ({kappa} 0.15 to 0.17); across the 185 ROBoto2 trials, RoB-BERT agreed with the human judgement on 67.4% ({kappa} 0.35) and 53.5% ({kappa} 0.20). Across all 419 assessments, domain agreement was 67.9% ({kappa} 0.29) for RoB-BERT, 65.0% ({kappa} 0.24) for Claude Fable 5.1, 52.7% ({kappa} 0.21) for GPT-6 Astra and 66.7% ({kappa} 0.26) for Gemini 4 Argon; overall agreement was 46.1% ({kappa} 0.16), 47.3% ({kappa} 0.17), 31.0% ({kappa} 0.03) and 46.5% ({kappa} 0.14), respectively. For domains the reference rated high risk, sensitivity was 22.2% for RoB-BERT, 23.1% for Claude Fable 5.1, 41.9% for GPT-6 Astra and 24.8% for Gemini 4 Argon, with specificity of 92.5%, 92.8%, 80.0% and 95.0%. On the 52 ROBoto2 trials rated by two assessors, the second assessors sensitivity for the reference assessors high-risk domains was 23.1% (specificity 90.3%) and RoB-BERTs was 30.8% (specificity 92.7%). RoB-BERT located 95.7% of its quotations verbatim in the report and cost US$0.005 per trial, 2% to 6% of the frontier models cost. ConclusionsRoB-BERT agreed with single human assessors at least as closely as two human assessors agreed with each other, and matched or exceeded frontier LLMs at a fraction of their cost. The results show the poor reliability of human assessors using RoB 2 and the need for consensus ratings, with RoB-BERT potentially serving as one rater.

papers.title: Asking Conversational Artificial Intelligence about Health and Subsequent Actions among Adults in Japan: A Cross-sectional Web Survey
papers.abstract: IntroductionPeople increasingly ask conversational artificial intelligence (AI) about health; however, how this relates to care seeking in Japan, where universal health coverage renders care accessible, remains unknown. This study described how many adults ask AI about health, why and when, what they do afterward, and how much they trust AI compared with other sources. MethodsThis two-stage cross-sectional survey employed a commercial web panel (October-November 2026). A screening survey of adults aged [≥]20 years (10,000 responses; 8,209 analyzed) estimated prevalence. A main survey of users (1,000 responses; 735 analyzed) asked about purposes, the most recent use and subsequent actions, and trust in seven information sources. Responses were weighted by sex and age. ResultsIn the past 6 months, 40.3% of adults (95% confidence interval, 39.3-41.4) asked conversational AI about health. The most recent use occurred before a medical visit for 39.0%, after a visit for 23.4%, and when no visit was being considered for 37.6%. Subsequently, 35.4% visited a medical facility; 12.8% (10.3-15.3) decided not to visit or postponed a visit (5.1% of all adults). Forgoing or delaying was more frequent among users with high trust in AI (trusting it completely or a lot; 22.5% vs. 10.9% among others). Among pre-visit users, it was less frequent with high trust in health professionals (16.7% vs. 30.9%) and did not clearly differ by trust in AI. Of users, 61.4% had high trust in health professionals and 14.3% in AI. ConclusionsIn Japan, approximately 4 in 10 adults asked AI about health, and 1 in 8 users forwent or delayed a visit. This was more common with high trust in AI; among pre-visit users, it was associated with low trust in health professionals. How trust in AI and health professionals relates to care seeking warrants further study.

papers.title: What Does an Agent-Run Clinic Cost? Protocol for a Prospective Observational Study of the Compute Cost of Completed Work in a Clinical Agent Fleet
papers.abstract: BackgroundDecisions about deploying large language model (LLM) agents in health care require the cost of completed work in production. Published evidence reports benchmark accuracy, benchmark-level cost, and time or financial outcomes for ambient documentation, and list prices alone do not determine the cost of completed work. To our knowledge, no deployed clinical agent fleet has published a measurement method that ties compute cost, latency, failures and retries to completed work. ObjectiveThis study aims to estimate the compute cost of completed work by the orchestrated clinical agents of a deployed LLM agent fleet over a 12-week window of production telemetry, using estimators, data-quality gates and an analysis plan fixed before any window data are extracted for the study. MethodsThe setting is a private outpatient clinic in London, United Kingdom, where wai, a multi-agent system supporting clinic operations, is deployed. The population is every run of the 20 orchestrated clinical documentation and decision-support agents starting between September 21 and December 13, 2026. The run store writes 2 records for every run, a non-terminal record before the model call and a terminal record after it, and has no attempt counter or parent-run link. Estimators defined on that structure cover cost per resolved execution and per completed intention, retry and failed-intention shares of compute, error and failure rates, latency, cost per draft offered for clinician review and a latency-cost frontier, by agent, task class and acceptance stratum. Cost is recorded in GBP pence, converted from provider-returned US dollar cost at a fixed rate and rounded per model call. The plan fixes weekly aggregation, small-cell suppression, bootstrap intervals over weeks, 2 prespecified comparisons, 5 sensitivity analyses and 4 data-quality gates whose failure converts an estimate into a bound or an unmeasured stratum. Two staff-level measures in an earlier version were dropped. Revenue, pricing, margin and staffing inference are excluded. ResultsThe measurement window opened on September 21, 2026, and closes on December 13, 2026, and telemetry is being recorded in routine operation. No window data had been extracted for this study at submission. Aggregate whole-table counts that include window records were extracted on November 19, 2026, for companion manuscripts and are disclosed. Extraction will begin no earlier than December 15, 2026, and the results are expected to be submitted for publication in 2027. ConclusionsThe compute cost of completed clinical agent work can be specified as estimators over the run-level telemetry this deployment records, provided paired recording rows are separated from retries, missing terminal states are bounded and rounding of recorded cost is reported. This protocol fixes those estimators, and the reporting consequence of each known instrumentation defect, before extraction. Trial RegistrationNone. The analysis plan will be registered on Open Science Framework Registries before any window data are extracted for this study. International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID)DERR1- 10.2196/ (to be assigned by the journal)

papers.title: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data
papers.abstract: BackgroundShort-term prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhosis is complicated by the competing risk of death from liver disease. We aimed to develop an interpretable model on region-wide routine data that predicts HCC while separating competing mortality, and to compare it with established risk scores. MethodsFrom a region-wide cohort of adults with cirrhosis in the Andalusian Population Health Database, we trained the model on 17,177 patients with a prediction date set 12 months before their outcome, between 2020 and 2023. From one year of electronic health records before that date (demographics, liver and chronic disease codes, and eight routine laboratory tests), an Explainable Boosting Machine without interaction terms classified the following 12 months as HCC, death or liver transplantation without HCC, or event-free. We evaluated it in 20 repeats of 5-fold cross-validation against a binary model, a model with pair interactions and a model using the full health record, all on the same folds. We then applied the cross-validated models, without retraining, at the first routine encounter at which aMAP or the Toronto HCC Risk Index could be computed, and compared them with the scores in patients followed forward under competing risks, with and without a 6-month washout and with each province left out of training in turn. Findings771 patients (4.5%) developed HCC within 12 months and 3,314 (19.3%) died or underwent liver transplantation without HCC (3,061 deaths, 253 transplants). In cross-validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for HCC was 0.734 (SD 0.018). A binary formulation, pairwise interactions and the full health record (more than 3,000 features) did not improve it; the full record lowered it by 0.024. At routine encounters the model discriminated 12-month HCC better than aMAP (time-dependent AUC 0.790 vs 0.688; difference +0.102, 95% CI +0.071 to +0.132) and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (0.761 vs 0.703; +0.057, +0.032 to +0.081), and remained better after excluding HCC diagnosed within 6 months (concordance difference +0.055 and +0.040) and when each of the eight provinces was left out of training. At equal group size, its high-risk group held as much HCC as the scores high-risk categories, with 20-28% fewer competing deaths. Its shape functions separated cancer-specific signal (AFP rising from 2 to 20 {micro}g/L, platelets below 150 x109/L) from liver failure (bilirubin above 51 {micro}mol/L, albumin below 35 g/L); a binary model showed only the first. InterpretationAn interpretable three-class model on routine data outperformed established scores for short-term HCC risk in cirrhosis, while showing whether each abnormal value points to cancer or to competing death. FundingThis work was supported by grants PID2023_152380OB and PRTR-C17.I1 from the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation; grant PMP24/00005 from the Instituto de Salud Carlos III (ISCIII); grant IE19_259 FPS from Consejeria de Salud y Consumo, Junta de Andalucia; and Horizon Europe (HORIZON), Marie Skodowska-Curie Actions Doctoral Networks (101226456-MLCARE). The funders had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation or writing of the report. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed to October 2026 for HCC risk prediction in cirrhosis with machine learning or risk scores. Machine-learning models usually outperform aMAP and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (THRI) in development data. They are mostly specific to one etiology (HBV or HCV), built on inputs not routinely available (elastography), black boxes explained post hoc, and evaluated without competing risks. A meta-analysis of models for non-viral liver disease found only one developed with a competing-risk approach, and rated all 14 included studies at high risk of bias (1). In prospective French cohorts analysed under competing risks, machine learning did not outperform aMAP (2). Added value of this studyIn a region-wide population of 17,177 adults with cirrhosis of all etiologies, we developed an interpretable three-class model on routine records: HCC, death or transplant, or event-free. Under competing risks, at the first encounter where each score could be computed, it ranked HCC better than aMAP and THRI, including after a 6-month washout. At the same group size it flagged as much HCC with 20-28% fewer patients who died first. The advantage held when each province was left out of training. Its shape functions are the whole model, not a post-hoc approximation, and separate markers of cancer from markers of liver failure. A binary model on the same data ranks HCC as well but folds the death signal into its single curve, as we show analytically. Implications of all the available evidenceSurveillance programmes can rank patients from data they already hold, with a model whose every contribution can be inspected. Modelling death as an outcome keeps patients unlikely to benefit off the high-risk list. External validation in other health systems, with local recalibration, is the next step.

papers.title: Germline Variant Profiling of NA12878 Chromosome 22 Identifies the Loss-of-Function CYP2D6*3 and *4 Pharmacogenetic Alleles
papers.abstract: The approach used in this project to call germline variants from short-read sequencing data forms the basis of a great deal of current human genetics, whether it be in population studies or in diagnostic testing. A full germline variant-calling workflow according to the GATK Best Practices was constructed and carried out using public whole-genome sequencing data from the reference sample NA12878. In order to comply with the limitations of a laptop (an Intel Core i3, 8 GB of RAM, Ubuntu via WSL2), the analysis was limited to chromosome 22. The reads for chromosome 22 were streamed directly from the 1000 Genomes high-coverage CRAM file (run ERR3239334), converted into paired FASTQ files, checked using FastQC and MultiQC, and then cleaned with fastp. The cleaned reads were aligned to a GRCh38 reference containing only chromosome 22 using BWA-MEM, after which they were sorted, duplicates were marked and the base quality scores were recalibrated before variants were called with GATK HaplotypeCaller. The GATK-recommended hard filters were applied separately to SNPs and indels, and the variants that passed these filters were annotated using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) and summarised with a Python script. From the 81,599 raw calls, 73,570 (90.2%) survived the filtering process, and the transition/transversion ratio for the SNPs that passed filtering was 2.04. Of the annotated variant alleles, 98.9% were already present in the catalogue, 734 affected the coding sequence in 270 genes, and no variant corresponded to a pathogenic entry in ClinVar. Examination using IGV verified the read support for the selected high-impact calls, including the variants that define the CYP2D6*3 and *4 alleles, consistent with the published genotype of NA12878. The main limitations were a reduced effective depth of 8.6x, resulting from an incomplete read-collation step which retained about 31% of the read pairs, and the use of a chromosome-only reference.

papers.title: Unified Machine Learning Model for Early Detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Frailty, and Fall Risk Using Multimodal Motor-Function Data
papers.abstract: BackgroundMild cognitive impairment (MCI), frailty, and fall risk often co-occur in older adults and share motor signs, yet they are screened and modeled separately. A unified model that predicts all 3 conditions from 1 sensor-based assessment could support earlier and more efficient screening, but such a model has rarely been developed or rigorously compared with separate models. ObjectiveThis study aimed to develop a unified machine learning model that predicts MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from sensor-based motor-function data, compare it with separate single-label models, explain its predictions, and test its robustness. MethodsCommunity-dwelling older adults (n=79) completed a multimodal motor-function assessment with the Mizzou Point-of-Care Assessment System (MPASS), covering gait, sit-to-stand, static balance, step-down, and reaction time, with some tasks repeated under a dual-task condition. With demographic and family-history data, this yielded 59 features. Unified classifier-chain and single-label models were built with 5 algorithms across 6 modeling stages, evaluated with repeated nested cross-validation, and compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and paired bootstrap tests. The final model was explained with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), and its robustness and the sufficiency of the sample size were tested with chain-input, chain-order sensitivity, domain-ablation, learning-curve, and power analyses. ResultsWith class weighting, the unified model had a higher mean AUC than the single-label models in 17 of 20 configurations and was never significantly worse, and it performed at least as well under nested model selection (0.615 vs 0.605; P=.58). The final extra trees model achieved a mean AUC of 0.645 (95% CI 0.569-0.722); discrimination was best for MCI (AUC 0.779, 95% CI 0.680-0.872) and lower for frailty (0.606) and fall risk (0.551). The model overestimated risk for all 3 outcomes, most for frailty. Most features (43/59, 73%), led by stride length, were shared across the 3 conditions, with consistent SHAP rankings in training and test participants ({rho}=0.99). Predicted frailty was the most important input for fall risk, and the 45 sensor features alone performed as well as the full model. Learning curves suggested that fall-risk prediction would benefit from more participants. ConclusionsA unified model predicted MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from one sensor-based assessment and performed as well as 3 separate models. It identified motor features shared across the conditions and used the link between frailty and fall risk. It performed best for MCI; with improvement for frailty and fall risk, recalibration, and external validation, such a model could support efficient screening of older adults for several conditions at once.

papers.title: Preferences for Accessible Health Information Among Deaf, Blind, and DeafBlind Adults: A Descriptive Qualitative Study
papers.abstract: OverviewPeople with sensory disabilities (e.g., deaf or hard-of-hearing [DHH], blind/low vision [BLV], and DeafBlind) encounter difficulties when accessing health information. These barriers impede people with sensory disabilities in obtaining, understanding, and using health information. This study aimed to identify barriers, facilitators, and preferred formats for health information to inform inclusive health communication, while addressing the variety of accessibility needs across people who are DHH, BLV, and DeafBlind. MethodsWe conducted a qualitative study using eight focus groups and eleven individual interviews with adults with different types of sensory disabilities. Interviews were conducted directly in English or American Sign Language, and recordings were professionally transcribed. Discussions explored experiences accessing health information, information source preferences, accessibility barriers, and reactions to different formats. Transcripts were coded using a hybrid thematic analysis process. Themes were generated through team discussions, code synthesis, and community partner feedback. ResultsWe developed three themes summarizing user-centered perspectives for designing consumer health information resources. Participants obtained health information from various sources including clinicians, family, friends, internet searches, and ChatGPT. Barriers included information overload, medical jargon, inaccessible website design, and communication breakdowns with clinicians. Preferences for health information formats differed across disability groups. Key recommendations included simplified language, structured layouts, and compatibility with assistive technologies (e.g., screen readers). ConclusionDespite varying accessibility needs across disabilities, participants agreed health information must be delivered through multiple accessible formats to meet diverse sensory needs. These findings are being used to develop health promotion checklists to enhance accessibility for people with sensory disabilities.

papers.title: REMI: A Free Tool for Truncated Proximity Searching in PubMed
papers.abstract: BackgroundPubMed is the most comprehensive freely available database for medical and health sciences publications, making it an essential platform for literature searching in budget-constrained settings (e.g. non-academic hospitals). However, unlike subscription platforms (e.g. Ovid MEDLINE), it cannot combine truncation with proximity operators. Searchers must therefore either enumerate every word form manually, risking missed variants, or fall back on Boolean AND, which retrieves many irrelevant records. We developed REMI (Related Expression Machine Identification), a free, open-source web application which emulates truncated proximity searching in PubMed. Case PresentationREMI was developed at Maastricht University Library. Through the NCBI E-utilities, it identifies the variants of truncated terms that occur in PubMed records. An iterative exclusion procedure, which reruns the search for each concept while excluding that concepts variants already found, surfaces progressively rarer forms. Users select relevant variants from frequency-ranked lists, and REMI combines them into native PubMed proximity clauses that can be documented, peer reviewed, and rerun without REMI. Performance of REMI was evaluated by comparison to four Ovid MEDLINE search strategies from published reviews. REMIs proximity search was able to identify all included articles found with the original Ovid MEDLINE query. ConclusionsREMI makes truncated proximity searching available in PubMed while keeping searches transparent, reliable, and reproducible, which particularly benefits searchers without access to subscription platforms. Because variant discovery is a sampling procedure, completeness is not guaranteed, and long searches require variant selection. Other libraries can use, host, or adapt the tool, however, native support in PubMed would remain the preferable solution.

papers.title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records
papers.abstract: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patients outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from[~] 350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

papers.title: A Blockchain-Enabled Federated Ensemble Framework for Privacy-Preserving Mortality Prediction Across Heterogeneous Healthcare Systems
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo test whether a smart contract that admits hospital-trained models to a shared mortality model only after peer hospitals verify their performance can exclude poisoned or substituted models, and at what cost. DesignRetrospective simulation study of a federated learning protocol. MethodologyIn the Blockchain-Enabled Federated Ensemble (BFE), hospitals committed SHA-256 digests of locally trained XGBoost and random-forest models to a Solidity contract; peers posted digest-bound validation AUROCs, and the contract admitted models with a median peer AUROC of at least 0.70. Admitted models were pooled by weighted logit averaging (BFE-PW) or stacking (BFE-Stack) with federated recalibration. Code and drafts were produced with an AI coding assistant under the authors supervision. SettingFour hospitals simulated from one academic centre with age, renal case-mix and laboratory-availability skew; a data-scarce regime keeping 5-20% of each hospitals training and validation patients; and a natural partition by care era. Participants425,215 adult admissions (186,103 patients; 2.35% in-hospital mortality) in MIMIC-IV v3.1, with predictors from the first 24 hours. InterventionsBFE against centralised, local-only, FedAvg, FedProx, median and Multi-Krum FedAvg and federated logistic regression, under seven attacks on training, attestation, recalibration and model delivery. Main outcome measuresAUROC and AUPRC (joint patient-clustered bootstrap), calibration, attack effects, gas and transactions. ResultsUnder gross label flipping, FedAvg lost 29% of its AUPRC while the contract excluded the poisoned models in every seed (Multi-Krum FedAvg was equally protected); all substituted models were detected, and collusion blocked release. A targeted flip of female deaths passed the gate and lowered sensitivity for deaths in women from 32.8% to 27.5%; poisoned recalibration inverted BFE-PW (AUROC 0.098) unless a median-of-sites recalibration was used (0.902). With large hospitals, BFE-PW matched FedAvg in AUROC (0.902) and BFE-Stack matched FedProx (0.907 and 0.906), below local-only (0.910) and centralised XGBoost (0.915), with lower AUPRC; with 5% of the data, BFE-PW exceeded local models (0.866 against 0.844). Pooled calibration hid two-fold under-prediction at one hospital (observed-to-expected ratio 2.13), which a local intercept corrected (0.93). One aggregation used 37 transactions and 3.3 million gas, rising roughly quadratically with consortium size. ConclusionsContract-enforced peer attestation gave auditable, automatic exclusion of grossly poisoned and substituted models at a small accuracy cost, but did not detect attacks that preserve validation discrimination. It is most useful for consortia of small hospitals that need a verifiable record of which models entered a shared tool. Plain language summaryHospitals can build better risk-prediction tools by learning from each others patients, but privacy rules make pooling records hard. Federated learning lets each hospital train on its own data and share only the model. A hospital could, however, contribute a bad model by error or on purpose, and no one can later check which models went into the shared tool. In our design each hospital records a digital fingerprint of its model on a blockchain, other hospitals test the model and record their scores, and a program on the blockchain lets the model in only if it scored well enough. We simulated groups of hospitals using 425,215 hospital stays. Key findingsO_LIThe shared tool was almost as accurate as standard federated learning, and better than each hospital alone when hospitals were small. C_LIO_LIModels trained on completely falsified outcomes were always kept out, and swapped models were always caught. C_LIO_LISubtler sabotage got through: hiding deaths in women made the tool miss more deaths in women, and falsifying the final adjustment step could reverse its predictions unless a robust adjustment was used. C_LIO_LIAt one hospital that measured fewer laboratory tests, the shared tool underestimated risk by about half; a simple local adjustment, made by that hospital alone, fixed it. C_LIO_LIRecording everything on a blockchain had a measurable cost that grows quickly as more hospitals join. C_LI The design makes the shared tool auditable, but it must be tested next on real data from separate hospitals.

papers.title: Building an Auditable Reference Standard for Clinical Information Extraction from Transesophageal Echocardiography Reports
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo develop an auditable, two-institution reference standard for intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) reports and evaluate whether reviewer disagreement identifies limitations in the underlying clinical information model. Materials and MethodsWe selected 300 reports (150 per institution) from 925 at the University of Pennsylvania and University of Washington using random sampling and enrichment for challenging documentation. Four trained abstractors applied a shared 39-variable V1 codebook. Independent paired comparisons included 297 reports; three historical reports contributed only to the final reference standard. Categorical agreement used exact agreement and unweighted Cohens{kappa} ; numeric left-ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) used exact agreement and mean absolute differences. Disagreements underwent structured expert adjudication and reason classification. Additional analyses assessed reviewer-pair, sampling-stratified, and population-weighted agreement. ResultsAmong 11,583 formal reviewer-comparison cells, 10,293 (88.9%) were resolved by reviewer agreement and 1,290 (11.1%) required targeted expert adjudication (1,289 tasks). Codebook/schema ambiguity (40.8%) and interpretation/classification differences (25.2%) together accounted for 66.0% of targeted tasks. Adjudication was concentrated in aortic dissection, valve type, and post-intervention findings. Categorical{kappa} ranged from 0.364 to 0.960 and was inversely correlated with targeted-adjudication burden (Spearman {rho}=-0.884; 95% CI, -0.955 to -0.734). Sampling-weighted{kappa} changed by no more than 0.05 for 32 of 35 categorical variables. DiscussionStructured adjudication identified recurring schema and interpretation challenges beyond individual abstraction errors, providing specific targets for information-model refinement. ConclusionAs NLP and LLM-based abstraction tools move toward clinical use, the reference standards used to evaluate them require comparably rigorous development, adjudication, and independent validation.
